title: Jesse Eisenberg Says Fans Aren’t Crazy With Him Because ‘There’s No Sexuality to My Work’: Life Is ‘Different’ When People ‘Want to Sleep With’ You
description: Jesse Eisenberg recently told the New Yorker that fans of his are “mostly fine” when he’s in public, a fact he attributes to his generally sexless
body:
Jesse Eisenberg recently told the New Yorker that fans of his are “mostly fine” when he’s in public, a fact he attributes to his generally sexless resume.

	“People are mostly fine,” he said to reporter Rachel Syme when asked if strangers ever interrupt him when they spot him working on scripts. (The “A Real Pain” actor told Syme that his typical schedule revolves around sitting at a branch of the New York Public Library, where he writes from nine to five). “It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work,” he continued. “I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.”
	

	Though, despite Eisenberg’s assertion, his “Fleishman Is in Trouble” co-star Claire Danes told Syme that people began to “rubberneck” when the two had a coincidental run-in on the street and stopped to chat. “People are very aware of him as a figure, even though he is so determined to be invisible,” she said.

	Elsewhere in the lengthy profile, Aaron Sorkin, who directed Eisenberg as a young Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” told the outlet that “I hardly know him at all,” noting that the actor reminds “me of Holden Caulfield, if that makes any sense. He has absolutely no patience for phonies.” 

	Eisenberg earned an Oscar nomination for the part, but has since been outspoken about his decision not to reprise the role in the director’s follow-up, “The Social Reckoning,” released earlier this year. “I’d be out at a bar, and a drunk guy would say, ‘Hey, I love your website,’” he told the New Yorker. “And as I’m pretending to laugh, I’d just wish all of the oxygen would leave my lungs, and that I would collapse on the floor in front of this guy and show him what he’s doing to me.”
	

	The actor-turned-director, who is currently promoting “The Debut,” his latest project, also spoke about creating “nonhierarchical” environments on his sets. “How could you be making a movie about a woman who’s an underdog, who no one notices, and then have a set where the people walking around feel like that?” he said. “You’d have to be so stupid and blind and compartmentalizing, in a psychopathic way, to write a movie about that and then perpetuate it.”

	“The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, stars Julianne Moore as Mona Friedman, a New Jersey housewife who auditions for a part in her local theater’s production of a fictional musical. After she’s cast as Miss Danielle, Friedman’s life begins to unravel as she becomes more consumed with the role and falls under the spell of director Jerry Blankenbuehler (Paul Giamatti). 

	“The Debut” opens from A24 in theaters on Dec. 11

schema.headline: Jesse Eisenberg Says Fans Aren’t Crazy With Him Because ‘There’s No Sexuality to My Work’: Life Is ‘Different’ When People ‘Want to Sleep With’ You

title: Candace Cameron Bure Says She Still Gets ‘Substantial’ ‘Full House’ Residuals and Wasn’t Surprised the Olsen Twins Skipped ‘Fuller House’: No One ‘Stayed Close’ With Them
description: Candace Cameron Bure appeared on the “McBride Rewind” podcast on Tuesday and discussed the “substantial” residuals she still gets from “Full House,
body:
Candace Cameron Bure appeared on the “McBride Rewind” podcast on Tuesday and discussed the “substantial” residuals she still gets from “Full House,” as well as why she wasn’t surprised that Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen didn’t return for the hit sitcom’s spin-off, “Fuller House.”

	“They’re substantial… I think it’s like quarterly,” Bure told host Josh McBride of the consistency of her “Full House” residuals, adding that every check is different, but “still substantial.” “I’m always happy when I open that check and deposit it,” she added.
	

	McBride then brought up Bure’s “Full House” co-star Jodie Sweetin, who made in April when the actress revealed she’d received a “one-cent check” from the show on the podcast. “She said she doesn’t get much now,” Bure said. “And I was like, ‘Jodie, you gotta check with your agent or you gotta call your bank.’ ’Cause I still get residuals.” 

	Speaking of the Olsen twins, Bure said that their decision not to appear on “Fuller House” was “a bummer” because “it would have been fun to have everybody back.” “But at the same time, it wasn’t surprising just because none of us really have stayed close with the girls,” Bure noted.

	She continued: “Not because anything went wrong or there was any bad blood. I just think they were kids. They were [filming from] 9 months old until they were 8 years old. They have very different memories than we do. Even me being 10 years older than them, I have significant, great, wonderful memories.”

	“They were babies. They probably don’t even remember half the stuff [we do],” she added. “They didn’t have the attachment to the crew and the people like we did being older. And they had such a successful fashion business. They haven’t been actors for a long time. They just haven’t been in that part of entertainment.”
	

	Sweetin played Stephanie Tanner and Bure played D.J. Tanner on “Full House,” which ran for eight seasons from 1987 to 1995. “Fuller House” ran for five seasons on Netflix, totaling nearly 80 episodes. Original cast members, including Bure, Sweetin, Andrea Barber, Scott Weinger, Bob Saget, Lori Loughlin, Dave Coulier and John Stamos, all returned for the series. Juan Pablo Di Pace, Adam Hagenbuch, John Brotherton, Michael Campion, Elias Harger and Soni Bringas also starred in the reboot.

schema.headline: Candace Cameron Bure Says She Still Gets ‘Substantial’ ‘Full House’ Residuals and Wasn’t Surprised the Olsen Twins Skipped ‘Fuller House’: No One ‘Stayed Close’ With Them

title: ‘South Park’ Season 29 Finale: ‘GTA 6’ Inspires Stan, Kyle and Cartman to Get to the Bottom of South America’s Power Outages
description: In the sixth and final episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America has once again been hit with major power outages — but this time it’s serio
body:
In the sixth and final episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America has once again been hit with major power outages — but this time it’s serious, considering “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally been released, which means the residents of the mountain town will stop at nothing to restore their Xboxes and PlayStations and continue playing the long-awaited video game.

	“Damn it, Mayor! We have waited over a decade for this game to come out,” proclaims one angry South American resident at the top of the episode. “Do you have any idea how ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ works? If it shuts up while it’s saving or during a mission, you lose everything.” The issue, though, is that the South American government has made a deal with a group of billionaire weenies, as was introduced in the season’s second episode, who are using the town’s energy to power their data centers.
	

	The town’s politicians have no idea what to do about the issue, but luckily for them, a group of angry townspeople barge into South American City Hall and proclaim they know who’s behind the outages: the Chinese. More specifically, the outages are the result of Chinese cyberattacks. Relieved, the town’s politicians let them believe this is the case — “Yes, you figured it out. It’s definitely cyber attacks by the Chinese” — as they begin to search for a Chinese spy who must be living in South America.

	But Butters has known the billionaires were to blame since the beginning, and confides in Stan, Kyle and Cartman. Oh, and a zombified Kenny (who got blown up by an e-bike during the season’s premiere) also makes a few appearances. Turns out, Kenny’s spirit can’t move on until the group figures out what’s going on and exposes all the corruption in South America — great timing for them, as they’ve all learned about the data centers and are ready to make a change. The gang takes this revelation to City Hall, where the politicians explain how it all began “with those damn e-bikes” and fear that the group of kids is going to blow their secret deal with the billionaires.
	

	But it wasn’t an e-bike that killed Kenny, says a still shrunken Randy who barges into City Hall. “We all did. We all share in the blame equally… When they changed the name of our town, we let it change us. We used force, took bribes, looked the other way, because we let them change South Park.”

	In the end, the mayor of South American addresses the town and owns up to her mistakes — kind of.

	“I owe you all an apology. Since the town changed its name, I’ve taken bribes. I’ve looked the other way, and I did make a deal with billionaires,” she says. “But I’ve learned that even though we must build data centers because there is a very real threat from the Chinese in the AI arms race, we can’t let that change who we are.”

	And so, the billionaire weenies help the town “do something we should have done a long time ago”: shoot Mr. Kim into space and out of South America. And with that, another season of “South Park” (and the first season with the new name of “South America”) comes to a close.

schema.headline: ‘South Park’ Season 29 Finale: ‘GTA 6’ Inspires Stan, Kyle and Cartman to Get to the Bottom of South America’s Power Outages

title: U2 Salutes Dolly Parton With Recreation of Their ‘Torn’ Duet in NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show
description: U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton as part of its halftime performance Wednesday night at the NFL‘s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game. The “duet” betw
body:
U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton as part of its halftime performance Wednesday night at the NFL‘s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game. The “duet” between a live Bono and a recording of Parton from last summer was the centerpiece of a highly promoted 10-minute set between halves of the contest between the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers, streamed exclusively on Netflix.

	U2 did not attempt to cram as many songs into their brief performance as other superstars have during halftime performances, getting in four. The band opened with an abridged “Sunday Bloody Sunday” and ended with “”Pride (in the Name of Love)” and Where the Streets Have No Name” — only squeezing in one song from their new album, the Parton duet, “Torn,” with images of Dolly projected onto three huge curtains that dropped around their stage at the 50-yard line.


	About a hundred extras took part in the performances — forming not a marching band, but a marching choir. U2 was also joined by the Womack Sisters, a vocal trio that has just been nominated for best new artist at the Grammys.


	The dancers first appeared as part of “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” which included an interpolation of the Supremes’ “Stop in the Name of Love,” rendered as something more somber, as performed by the Womack Sisters, to better fit in with U2’s theme of civil war. Bono repeated the “torn” part of that early ’80s anthem as a segue into the song “Torn,” as he and the spectral Parton harmonized on the recent song about a family at war. After one last look at Dolly, the curtains dropped to the field and the dancers formed three concentric circles around the band’s platform, repeating the familiar strains of of “Where the Streets Have No Name” and then “Pride (in the Name of Love)” as the Womacks joined U2 on stage.


	Technically, five U2 songs made their way into the set, as eagle-eyed or -eared U2 fans were able to catch a bit of “American Obituary” during “Sunday Bloody Sunday.” The song, which appeared on a recent EP from the band, references the killing by ICE of Renee Good.


	The four key songs were just condensed enough that U2’s members were actually able to use part of their allotted 10 minutes walking to the stage at the beginning and walking back out through the assembled marchers at the end, in casual yet dramatic fashion.
	


	Some political subtext relevant to the times was seen by at least a small subset of fans in that assemblage of material, although it hardly would have been evident to less hardcore fans or strictly NFL-oriented viewers. That was evident in connecting “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” about the Irish conflicts, with the “American Obituary” snippet. Then, bringing in the Parton song might have been a no-brainer anyway, as her part on the duet was said to be the last studio recording ever made by the superstar before she died in August. But beyond that, the theme of the tune has been described as reflecting the kinds of squabbles that occur among families when relatives get together for Thanksgiving and air their political differences around the dinner table, with Parton playing the role of the mother who wants everyone to mend what drives them apart.

	Although this was the NFL’s first such Thanksgiving Eve halftime show, it is in a very recent tradition of superstars doing holiday halftimes; the previous ones have just been for Christmas. On Dec. 24, 2024, a Baltimore/Houston game featured a performance by the latter city’s hometown favorite, in the “Beyoncé Bowl.” For Christmas Day 2025, the NFL enlisted Snoop Dogg for a “Holiday Halftime Party.” No plans have been announced as of yet for a Christmas halftime extravaganza from the NFL.
	

	U2’s camp reportedly approached the NFL themselves with the idea of doing a Thanksgiving halftime show — obviously timed to capitalize not just on families gathered around the TV before a holiday, but, from U2’s perspective, following closely on the heels of the Nov. 13 release of “Carnaval de Luz,” the band’s first album of new material in nine years. The album debuted at No. 4 on the latest Billboard 200 chart.

	It was U2’s third tango with the NFL, albeit its first in two decades. The Irish band famously did the Super Bowl halftime show in 2002, with an emphasis on honoring the victims of 9/11. In 2006, the group performed in celebration of the opening of the Louisiana Superdome after Hurricane Katrina.

	The group has kept up a heavy cycle of broadcast and streaming promotions before and since the new album release, including a surprise opening to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony at L.A.’s Peacock Theatre on Nov. 14, which is being edited into a special to be broadcast Dec. 8 on ABC.

	On Monday, U2 announced the itinerary for a 15-date tour of North American stadiums in 2027, on top of already announced shows in Central America and Europe. The tour has them returning to the site of their NFL performance, SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., presumably for much longer performances, on oct. 1-2, 2027.

schema.headline: U2 Salutes Dolly Parton With Recreation of Their ‘Torn’ Duet in NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show

title: Colman Domingo Responds to Post Telling Oscar Pundits Not to Add His ‘Michael’ Performance to Predictions: ‘Who Hurt You?’
description: Colman Domingo is firing back at a critic of “Michael” and his performance as Joe Jackson, which some members of the film press forecast will earn
body:
Colman Domingo is firing back at a critic of “Michael” and his performance as Joe Jackson, which some members of the film press forecast will earn him major nominations this awards season.

	“Hot take: Awards prognosticators adding Colman Domingo for Michael, you really don’t need to add a mid performance/bad movie. You really don’t,” posted a user to X on Wednesday. Domingo kept his response short, replying simply: “Who hurt you?”
	

	In the musical biopic, released back in April, Domingo plays the domineering father of pop superstar Michael Jackson. His turn as the patriarch of the Jackson family earned him praise from critics when the film first hit theaters, so much so that several awards prognosticators, as the X user wrote, are predicting Oscar and Golden Globe nominations for the actor.

	Ahead of the film’s premiere, the “Euphoria” actor told The Wall Street Journal that he focused on finding the father’s “humanity” in order to play him. “He created some of the most iconic artists that have ever walked this earth,” he added. “What goes into the making of that man?” Of the alleged abusiveness of the father, Domingo said: “I will say that he chastised his children. It’s always going to be arguable what’s right and a great method.”

	Because of the allegations surrounding Michael Jackson’s alleged sexual abuse of children (which the executors of the Jackson estate, who produced the film, have maintained are false), the film was controversial even before it hit theaters. Speaking about the film with Variety in Nov. 2024, Domingo said that “anything surrounding those ideas about him never came into play with me… It’s about the character, more than anything. And the idea of working with the estate, Antoine Fuqua and Jaafar Jackson — who is exceptional.”
	

	Alongside Domingo, the film stars Jackson’s nephew Jafaar Jackson as the titular pop star, Nia Long as his mother Katherine, Miles Teller as lawyer John Branca, Laura Harrier as Suzanne de Passe, Jamal R. Henderson as Jermaine Jackson, Tre Horton as Marlon Jackson, Rhyan Hill as Tito Jackson, Joseph David-Jones as Jackie Jackson and Jessica Sula as La Toya Jackson. 

	While the film holds the record for the highest-grossing biopic ever made, Variety exclusively reported that it was not submitted for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards.

schema.headline: Colman Domingo Responds to Post Telling Oscar Pundits Not to Add His ‘Michael’ Performance to Predictions: ‘Who Hurt You?’

title: ‘The Squirrel’ Review: An Endearing Futuristic Dramedy, Finland’s Oscar Entry Makes a Case for Organic Love in the Age of Automation
description: If Finnish master Aki Kaurismäki, with his measured emotional register and stoic humor, were to ever make a science-fiction film taking a page from
body:
If Finnish master Aki Kaurismäki, with his measured emotional register and stoic humor, were to ever make a science-fiction film taking a page from a seminal text in the genre like “Blade Runner,” it may resemble Markus Lehmusruusu’s endearing dramedy “The Squirrel.”

	Before one learns anything else about how the film’s unspecified, seemingly idyllic future operates, Lehmusruusu reveals that even the intimate act of masturbation has been automated here. The opening scene sees Pasi (Miro Lopperi), a lanky man in his early 30s whose face radiates heartwarming innocence, step into a rose-colored room for a machine to help him “regulate his hormones.”
	

	Rather than offering a montage, an introductory title card, or an expository speech on the mechanics of this era, the astute writer-director (with a background mostly in local episodic TV) allows for the most essential of those details to surface as we follow Pasi’s mundane day as part of a team designing the latest robotic pet: a dog that’s only slightly more sophisticated versions of those Poo-Chi toy pups from the early 2000s. 

	The tone, from the onset, is charmingly deadpan, with the characters acting oblivious to the absurdism. Again, if Kaurismäki needs a homegrown successor, he may have one in Lehmusruusu. Following a September premiere at Fantastic Fest, the film has been picked up for North American distribution by Obscured Releasing.

	Every aspect of everyone’s life is monitored under the guise of maintaining collective comfort and happiness above individual satisfaction. Swear words are discouraged by the ominous artificial voice that’s always listening, and even bending machines decide whether one should consume caffeine or not. Each person wears a bracelet that keeps track of their health — not too far from what smart watches already do today. In Lehmusruusu’s vision, these devices and the information they collect have already become instruments of control.
	

	This emotionally sanitized world emerges visually via the formalism of cinematographer Max Smeds’s elegant framing, showcasing the symmetrical spaces and parallel lines in the infrastructure of this reality: escalators at a subway station, the stairs in the building were Pasi works, or the homogenously designed apartment complexes. For the interior of Pasi’s flat, production designer Michael Randel creates a mostly white, brightly lit, nearly antiseptic space where chaos seems unfathomable. Likewise, the muted colors of the costumes enhance the feeling of existing in an oppressively solemn, lifeless timeline.

	Pasi’s understanding of this post-stress world, where all his needs are met and nothing unexpected ever occurs, is upended when he comes across the titular rodent one night on his way home. The encounter, which he must report, also introduces him to investigator Emilia (Mimosa Willamo). Attraction is instant between the two, but neither makes a move. Lehmusruusu makes clear that a crime like adultery is punished with a procedure that erases the perpetrator’s memory, implying that spontaneous love might also be off limits.

	The streamlined conception of the narrative, with no intel about the characters’ past or specifics on how people are raised in this society to become model citizens, works because it frees the film from having to explicitly justify every choice. Instead, it distills the ideas into situations that offer enough context for the point to come across without being burdened by lengthy explanations. As a bridge to the past, Lehmusruusu provides Jimi (Hannu-Pekka Björkman), a longtime employee at Pasi’s job with knowledge about the animals that once roamed the earth and what’s beyond the bubble that humanity (or at least this segment of it) have trapped themselves in.

	It’s only after he secretly adopts the squirrel that Pasi begins to comprehend that it’s precisely the randomness of an organic life, at times acting and reacting on instinct (even if against one’s best interests) that makes the experience of being alive worthwhile, or at least interesting. Those in charge seek to prevent unpredictability at all costs, stopping people from making mistakes, but also from finding greater fulfilment. The ethos that runs through Lehmusruusu’s narrative aligns with the approach to bringing the squirrel character to the screen — the animal is mostly played by four real rescue squirrels under the care of a trainer (with some assistance from a puppet and minimal CGI).
	

	The disarming faint smile that appears on Lopperi’s face when Pasi plays with said squirrel — a playful interaction that an artificial creature cannot match — turns into a frown as the little furball shows signs of heartache. Lehmusruusu takes this newly found relationship between man and nature as the vehicle to encourage Pasi to seek a human bond, not in an intellectual manner, but surrendering to his inherent need for companionship and physical touch. An effectively minimalist, offbeat delight, “The Squirrel” makes a case for organic love in the age of automation.

schema.headline: ‘The Squirrel’ Review: An Endearing Futuristic Dramedy, Finland’s Oscar Entry Makes a Case for Organic Love in the Age of Automation

title: Microdrama Revenue to Hit $20 Billion in 2026, but Profits Outside China Remain Thin, Media Partners Asia Report Finds
description: Global microdrama revenue will climb 24% to $20 billion in 2026, but outside China the business has yet to prove it can make reliable money, accord
body:
Global microdrama revenue will climb 24% to $20 billion in 2026, but outside China the business has yet to prove it can make reliable money, according to new research from Media Partners Asia.

	The Asia-focused research and advisory firm’s second annual study of the sector, “The Microdrama Economy 2026,” projects the market will reach $32 billion by 2031, on annual growth of 9.8%. MPA’s figures measure spending by viewers, advertisers and brands before app stores and payment processors take their cut. Outside China, they count only dedicated microdrama apps and their web storefronts, not general social media feeds.
	

	China still dominates. The country will generate $15.2 billion this year, or 76% of the global total, after revenue jumped 90% in 2025. MPA expects growth there to cool to 6.7% annually as viewing levels off, taking Chinese revenue to $21 billion by 2031. The firm’s China figure is narrower than the National Radio and Television Administration’s RMB100 billion ($15 billion) estimate for 2025, which also counts producer outlays on AI models and platform investment.

	Free, ad-supported viewing overtook paid viewing in China in 2025. Advertising will make up 69% of the country’s microdrama revenue this year and 79% by 2031. ByteDance, which operates Hongguo and Douyin, takes 56% of Chinese revenue, and ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou together command 82%.

	Dedicated apps outside China will earn $4.87 billion in 2026, a third more than last year, with MPA forecasting $11 billion by 2031 on annual growth of 17.7%. The U.S. remains the biggest single market at $1.71 billion, though that is 2% lower than in 2025. Asia-Pacific excluding China, at $1.44 billion, is set to overtake the U.S. in 2029.
	

	India, at $322 million, now outranks Japan and Korea as the biggest market in Asia after China. It is also the fastest-growing, with revenue more than tripling this year. Local players Kuku TV and Story TV both roughly tripled their takings, and JioStar launched its microdrama service Tadka on JioHotstar in April. India is the only big market where local platforms lead, selling cheap subscriptions that bypass app-store billing. JioStar’s existing streaming audience has reduced its need to pay for new users, and the company is now turning to retention and growing ad revenue.

	Revenue is concentrated. ReelShort, DramaBox–GoodShort, Kunlun and NetShort together generate 65% of the total outside China, and each is either owned or financed from China. DramaBox and GoodShort announced a merger on Oct. 31, the first such deal among the sector’s top players, partly so the two would stop outbidding one another for advertising. Fox, Versant and NBCUniversal are among the U.S. media companies that have bought minority stakes in the sector, while India’s and Korea’s biggest local platforms are gearing up to go public.

	Some homegrown companies take on the Chinese-owned apps directly, among them Korea’s Vigloo and Fuji TV’s FOD Short in Japan. MPA sees their edge in what the Chinese apps don’t have: built-in audiences, homegrown IP and talent, and a way to bill viewers without payment cards. Japanese and Korean broadcasters, studios and telcos mostly work as producers. Across Southeast Asia, telcos have sold heavily discounted passes to build reach, though MPA said it is unclear whether these bring in new paying customers or simply shift existing ones to a cheaper channel.

	TikTok sits on all sides of the market. It sells advertising to the apps, carries their series and competes with them through its free app PineDrama. In Southeast Asia, ByteDance is repeating its China playbook, building audiences with free, ad-funded apps before cashing in. MPA expects TikTok to become a major player in the U.S. and Southeast Asia alike by 2031. YouTube stays open to creators and studios, while Meta mainly serves as the place where apps find new users. Even so, MPA doesn’t expect free platforms to push out the paid apps, which control the IP and the billing relationship with paying customers.
	

	Profits are the sticking point. For each dollar of revenue generated outside China, 56 cents goes to marketing and another 18 cents to app stores and payment processors. In a typical month, just one in 12 users or so pays anything. The two largest groups each bring in more than $1 billion a year, yet DramaBox posted a 3.2% net margin in fiscal 2025. ReelShort lost $12 million in 2025 before swinging to a profit of roughly $8 million in the January-March quarter of 2026.

	“Demand for microdrama is established in every major market, but outside China this is still an emerging business, and it has yet to show that it can earn a durable profit,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and executive director of Media Partners Asia. “The leading apps spend more than half of their revenue to acquire viewers, and most of those viewers do not pay. Consolidation has begun, and China has already moved to free, advertising-funded viewing. The companies that endure will be those that retain their viewers, bill them directly and invest in titles worth returning to.”

	AI is reshaping supply far faster than demand. By MPA’s count, new titles listed on non-China apps will surge from around 100,000 in 2025 to 440,000 this year, with the AI-generated share climbing from 15% to 75%. Each listing represents a single title in a single language on a single app, so a series that runs in multiple languages or across multiple apps shows up more than once. Producing a title with AI costs roughly 10% of what a Los Angeles shoot would.

	Audiences have been slower to switch. Live-action titles hold most of the top 50 spots on five of the six non-China platforms MPA tracks. In China, about nine in 10 titles released in 2026 are AI-made, but they bring in just 20% of the year’s revenue.

	“What decides a platform’s economics is how many of its titles earn back the marketing spent on them,” said Myat Pan Phyu, MPA’s lead analyst for microdrama and vertical video. “That favors companies with established IP, stars and audiences of their own, which is why local broadcasters, studios and telecom operators matter to the next phase.”

	Payments may shift the math. Apple and Google process 65% of the revenue earned outside China, though legal rulings and fresh legislation in the U.S., Japan and Korea have cleared the way for web payments. Direct billing can lift margins, although the savings depend on each market’s fees and payment route. MPA expects payments made outside the app stores, including through India’s UPI system, to deliver roughly half of the growth outside China in 2027.

schema.headline: Microdrama Revenue to Hit $20 Billion in 2026, but Profits Outside China Remain Thin, Media Partners Asia Report Finds

title: ‘Four Seasons In Java’ Review: Indonesia’s Oscar Submission Is a Gorgeous, Slow-Burning Thriller With Elements of Magical Realism
description: A gloriously executed slow burn of a suspense thriller, mixed with magical realism and other genre tropes, “Four Seasons In Java” connects the them
body:
A gloriously executed slow burn of a suspense thriller, mixed with magical realism and other genre tropes, “Four Seasons In Java” connects the themes and concerns of Indonesian writer-director Kamila Andini’s previous films in an exhilarating and emotionally moving way. It follows a formerly incarcerated, sexually abused woman who returns to her remote Javanese village after 20 years and finds the men behind her ordeal still in charge. Issues of female power, self-determination and challenges to the patriarchy connect with questions about trauma, memory and what it takes to reclaim home and identity. After 2021’s TIFF Platform Prize winner “Yuni,” “Java” marks the second of Andini’s films to be selected as Indonesia’s international feature Oscar submission.
	

	When Pertiwi (a magnificent Putri Marino in the present; Shofia Shireen in flashbacks) returns to her parents’ rural home in the shadow of majestic Mount Bromo, she is far from the shy, obedient 16-year-old schoolgirl her mother remembers. No longer afraid or ashamed, she is a fighter, determined to stand up for herself and others.

	In contrast, the dynamic at Pertiwi’s parents’ home has not changed: Her weak-willed, alcoholic father (Iswadi Pratama) still racks up gambling debts and her mother continues to make excuses for him. Unwelcome in the village, Pertiwi sets about assembling an alternative family from fellow outcasts and brings them to live with her in an abandoned building outside the village limits. Together with former sex worker and café operator Mak Ira (iconic Indonesian actress Christine Hakim, chewing the scenery a bit here) and village madman/high school friend Kuntet (Dwika Pradnyana), who shares her interest in electrical engineering, Pertiwi develops a catering business, patronized by her one-time boyfriend Bisma (Arya Saloka), and also works on solar generators.
	

	It takes some time for Pertiwi to tell her loved ones about what happened to her (spoiler alert/trigger warning: she was raped), but Andini powerfully uses all the elements of cinema to indicate her severe trauma. Certain people — in particular, village headman/former teacher Fajar (Totos Rasiti) — and places trigger Pertiwi’s memories, which first return as quick, jagged images crackling with horror-movie energy and later as entire devastating scenes that she seems to be able to watch as if they were a vintage TV show. At other times, she feels as if she is being followed by a heavy-breathing monster with sharp claws that only she can see.

	When Pertiwi witnesses some young village men sexually abusing deaf schoolgirl Raras (Hanna Aretha O. Ginting), she literally cracks heads and determines to shine a light on the village’s dark doings. Her activism makes her return even more of a threat to Faraj and his patron Sapto (Doni Kus Indarto), the village’s richest man, who aims to keep his clan in power in whatever unscrupulous way he can.

	Andini creates many striking visual metaphors. She juxtaposes the majestic nature surrounding the village and the succor that Pertiwi draws from it (her name means Mother Nature) with the evil deeds of Sapto’s family, the village headman and the corrupt police, that take place in dimly lit interiors and darkened spaces. She also contrasts the technology and light that Pertiwi and Kuntet create with their solar energy with the run-down electric plant, long exploited by Sapto and his henchmen, and the wounds it renders in nature. The light metaphor is also cleverly extended into a deus ex machina reveal as well as a magical realist ending.

	Although certain scenes many have the look of a Western, as when Pertiwi and Bismas ride through fields, flats and forests, Andini also grounds the film in Javanese culture and tradition. The second of two scenes of traditional dancing and gamelan playing led by a shaman’s family, who are also treated as outcasts by the village officials, evokes a powerful magic that becomes a form of resistance. The striking, mood-setting, percussive score by Ricky Lionardi and Bottlesmoker deserves a shout out amongst the rest of the remarkable tech package.

	The chief criticism is that the film is so packed with characters and incident that some story arcs and characters seem neglected and not as well integrated into the overall narrative. This is particularly the case with Pertiwi’s reunion with her fellow ex-prisoners and a striking scene at a Jakarta club where Pertiwi reads a poem accompanied by howling punk band. This critic would welcome a mini-series about Pertiwi and her mates in Jakarta.

title: Crypto Exec Constance Wang Slams Her Portrayal in Netflix Series ‘The Altruists’ as ‘Racist’ and ‘Very Stereotypical’
description: Former FTX COO Constance Wang is calling out Netflix’s “The Altruists.” Wang took to social media on Wednesday to respond to whether the streamer h
body:
Former FTX COO Constance Wang is calling out Netflix’s “The Altruists.” Wang took to social media on Wednesday to respond to whether the streamer had consulted her about what she describes as a “very stereotypical” portrayal of her by actress Madison Hu.

	“People have asked whether Netflix consulted me. They didn’t,” wrote Wang on X. “One conversation would at least have saved Madison Hu, who plays me, the trouble of putting on a Chinese accent I don’t have. It feels very stereotypical, then again, it’s Netflix. What did we expect?”
	

	On Monday, Wang wrote that she and others who had worked at Alameda Research and FTX, the companies the show focuses on, recognized “little beyond the names” in the Graham Moore-created limited series.

	“My expectations were low, but I’m still surprised it’s this bad,” she continued. “In short, the story has nothing to do with what actually happened at FTX or Alameda… Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.”

	“The Altruists,” the Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner-led drama inspired by the real-life story of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, hit the streamer on Nov. 19. Per the show’s official logline, “The Altruists” tells the story of Bankman-Fried (Boyle) and Ellison (Garner), “two hyper-smart, ambitious young idealists who tried to remake the global financial system in the blink of an eye — before they were accused of stealing $8 billion.”

	Bankman-Fried founded the failed FTX cryptocurrency exchange in 2019, before ultimately being sentenced to 25 years in prison when a federal jury convicted him on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to the collapse of his cryptocurrency company and related hedge fund. The U.S. government alleged that Bankman-Fried had cheated investors and customers out of upwards of $10 billion through FTX and his crytpo trading firm Alameda Research.
	

	Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research, a trading firm affiliated with FTX, and was in a relationship with Bankman-Fried.

title: ‘Baahubali,’ ‘RRR’ Tech Chief C.V. Rao, New SMPTE Fellow, on Why Indian Filmmakers Shouldn’t Depend on Overseas Facilities
description: C.V. Rao, who helped shape the production and post-production pipelines behind S.S. Rajamouli‘s “Baahubali” films and “RRR,” has become the first t
body:
C.V. Rao, who helped shape the production and post-production pipelines behind S.S. Rajamouli‘s “Baahubali” films and “RRR,” has become the first technologist from South India to be named a Fellow of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE).

	Rao, chief technology officer at Hyderabad-based Annapurna Studios, describes the honor as one that comes with added responsibility, along with a chance to learn from senior figures across the global SMPTE community.
	

	“It also reflects the tremendous technical talent available in India,” Rao tells Variety. “We have developed strong capabilities in adopting and implementing advanced filmmaking technologies, and we believe the next opportunity is to contribute more actively to innovation, technology development and international standards.”

	“Baahubali” brought challenges well beyond what the studio had expected. The scale of the production demanded major upgrades in grading, processing power, storage, bandwidth and technical staff. For “Baahubali 2,” the team set up a dedicated peer-to-peer link between Hyderabad and Los Angeles to send large volumes of material straight to Imax. The experience also led to the launch of ANR Sound & Vision, a one-stop post facility that takes projects from data management and editing through VFX, sound, grading and final mastering.

	The Dolby Cinema version of “RRR” had its roots in Las Vegas, where a Dolby Cinema demo at NAB led to talks with cinematographer K.K. Senthil Kumar, who pitched the idea to Rajamouli.

	“We had to travel to Germany for the Dolby Cinema processing of ‘RRR,’ which raised an important question: why should Indian filmmakers depend on overseas facilities for these capabilities?” Rao says. “That experience became a major motivation for establishing Dolby Cinema processing capabilities at Annapurna Studios.”
	

	Rao points out that India had skilled VFX artists and capable post houses well before either film. What Rajamouli’s productions brought was a new order of scale and complexity, which pushed studios to grow their capabilities, strengthen their teams and get departments working together more closely. Both films also relied on international partners. Attempting projects of that size entirely within India 10 years earlier would have been far tougher, he says, given the gaps in specialized infrastructure, processing capacity and experience at the time.

	“The most significant impact was the confidence these projects created across the industry,” Rao says. “They demonstrated that Indian studios could handle increasingly complex work and encouraged greater investment in our technical ecosystem.”

	Rao started out as a graphic designer and 3D artist. From there he worked his way through documentary and feature editing, scanning, lab work, visual effects and color grading. That time spent across departments taught him where crews run into trouble during the shoot and in post, and at Annapurna he has used it to find weak spots in workflows and build infrastructure around what productions actually need.

	“We have always believed that understanding the filmmaker’s requirements is just as important as understanding the technology itself,” he says.

	Annapurna has put money into virtual production and one of India’s largest motion-capture stages. Interest is growing, but uptake has lagged expectations. During COVID, the studio saw virtual production as a way for filmmakers to stay inside controlled environments and cut down on location work and travel. The format, though, demands heavy preparation: digital sets have to be built, and camera moves and lighting mapped out, before anyone shoots a frame.

	“In our industry, approvals and shooting schedules often get finalized very late,” Rao says. “Even when filmmakers are interested, there may not be enough time to prepare everything properly. Under these circumstances, conventional shooting becomes the easier option.”

	Motion capture is gaining ground on complex action scenes, digital characters and performance-driven VFX. Rao expects both technologies to become standard tools once more productions have hands-on experience and learn where they genuinely save time.
	

	On infrastructure, he maintains that Indian facilities hold their own against established international hubs and can access most of the same advanced technology. Several major Indian productions now finish large chunks of their post work at home. Where India trails is research and development. Mature markets, he says, benefit from close collaboration among studios, technology companies, research institutions and creatives, while India needs to spend more on homegrown technology and on testing new workflows.

	“We strongly believe infrastructure alone cannot deliver quality,” Rao says. “The knowledge, experience and creativity of the professionals behind it make the real difference.”

	Annapurna has also set up Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos mastering facilities. Rao finds big-budget productions increasingly sold on premium formats, while mid-budget filmmakers are still weighing whether they pay off commercially. With streaming and high-end TVs giving audiences quality viewing at home, he sees premium theatrical formats as a reason to get people back into cinemas.

	“However, there needs to be better alignment between mastering capabilities and theatrical exhibition infrastructure,” Rao says. As more premium-format screens open across India, he expects producers to commit to these formats earlier in their release plans.

	AI is already proving useful in concept development, storyboarding, previsualization, restoration and repetitive VFX tasks, letting teams test ideas faster and automate slow work.

	“However, storytelling, performances, emotional expression and final artistic decisions must remain under human creative control,” he says.

	He sees AI working alongside existing tools rather than replacing them. Complex digital characters driven by performance may still need precise motion capture, with AI handling supporting jobs.

	Whether any of this lowers costs depends on the project. Virtual production can trim location, travel and scheduling expenses, but it requires investment in infrastructure, digital assets and prep, and without proper planning it can end up costing more. AI is getting easier for smaller filmmakers to access, yet consistent professional results still call for skilled teams, computing power and quality control.

	“We believe smaller productions can benefit from shared facilities and specialized technology services rather than investing in expensive infrastructure independently,” Rao says.
	

	Having overseen technical pipelines for more than 500 feature-film deliveries, Rao traces most post-production trouble back to poor planning. The most frequent error is bringing post teams in too late, when VFX, sound, grading, data management and delivery specs should ideally be on the table in pre-production. Late creative changes are the other big problem. Changes come with the territory, he acknowledges, but major revisions near delivery put artists and technicians under enormous strain.

	“Teams may need to work extended hours, repeat completed tasks and rush important processes to meet deadlines,” Rao says. “This creates unnecessary stress, increases costs and can sometimes compromise the quality of the final product.”

	For India to land complete high-end international productions, Rao wants a friendlier business climate, consistent government policy, competitive incentives and simpler approvals, along with deeper partnerships with global studios and more spending on research, training and integrated facilities.

	“The opportunity is to position India not merely as a cost-effective outsourcing destination, but as a reliable creative and technical partner capable of handling complete productions to international standards,” he says.

	Training is part of that equation. Rao wants studios to offer structured internships and mentorship, educational institutions to rework curricula alongside working professionals, and government to back specialized training centers and research.

	As an SMPTE Fellow, he plans to take part in technical discussions where India’s experience can help. An industry that works across many languages and production scales, under demanding workflows, has lessons to offer in digital cinema, post-production and data management, he says. He frames the fellowship as a two-way exchange, bringing ideas from global engineers and researchers back home in return.

	Looking five years out, Rao expects AI, real-time rendering, virtual production and motion capture to reshape filmmaking as they increasingly converge. Annapurna will keep upgrading its infrastructure, exploring new workflows and training teams, judging each new technology on whether it solves real production problems rather than on novelty.

	“Ultimately, we believe technology investments should be driven by the value they bring to filmmaking, not simply by technological advancement itself,” Rao says.

title: YNW Melly Wants Technology Search Thrown Out, Judge Approves
description:
YNW Melly
                          Bid to Have Evidence From iPhone Thrown Out Approved
body:
YNW Melly
                          Bid to Have Evidence From iPhone Thrown Out Approved
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 25, 2026
                            4:51 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 25, 2026
                                8:14 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              YNW Melly's trying a ton of different legal tactics to win his upcoming murder trial ... including getting evidence obtained from an iPhone thrown out -- and the judge signed off on his request.
      
    
              Here's the deal ... last month, YNW Melly filed legal documents arguing that data obtained from his Instagram, Snapchat, Google and iPhone obtained by investigators back in 2024 should be disregarded -- claiming the search warrant obtained was overbroad and no probable cause established in the affidavit could justify the search and seizure.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              His side also alleged that a detective accessed requested material illegally ... claiming the judge in Melly's first trial even raked the guy over the coals for not acting "in good faith" when he "conducted an illegal search" of the data.
      

              Prosecutors fired back, arguing investigators didn't do anything wrong by legally obtaining previously suppressed evidence after securing another warrant for that evidence.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              Ultimately, the judge sided with Melly ... ruling they can't use the evidence at trial.
      
    
              As you know ... Melly is accused of killing YNW Sakchaser and YNW Juvy back in 2018. YNW secured a mistrial in 2023 ... though he's remained locked up in the years since, awaiting his retrial.

title: Joan Smalls Confirms Fall Out with Candice Swanepoel Over Tom Brady Romance
description:
Joan Smalls
                          Candice Swanepoel & I Are Through ...
body:
Joan Smalls
                          Candice Swanepoel & I Are Through ...
                          Tom Brady Drama Ended Our Friendship!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 25, 2026
                            5:51 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Joan Smalls is confirming that her friendship with Candice Swanepoel is completely over ... admitting Tom Brady played a major part in the unraveling.
      
    
              The model and TV personality dove into her relationship with Swanepoel on an episode of "The Cutting Room Floor" podcast ... confirming she took 0 pics with Candice at this year's Victoria's Secret fashion show.
      
    
              When asked if that means the friendship is truly over, Smalls said she already said as much on social media when she wrote, "I’m not friends with backstabbers."
      

              Smalls was then asked if Tom Brady was the cause ... and she admitted he was.
      
    
              She said, "Unfortunately, that was the catalyst. I was seeing this person for a period of eight months. The internet described it as a ‘fling.’”
      
    
              Smalls said Swanepoel told her she needed to talk to her ... and she had a feeling it was about Brady -- which she didn't appreciate because she says Swanepoel helped her write text messages to the NFL star.
      
    
              As for how that convo went ... Smalls said, "She came across as justifying her action, that what I had wasn’t valid or it was casual. She started diminishing my experience to make herself feel better about the situation, which I think is what infuriated me."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              She added, “As my friend to -- one -- diminish me or devalue my friendship so much that you didn’t have consideration toward my feeling or my hurt. It was this whole attitude of, 'I’m an adult, I don’t need permission.'”
      
    
              While many have called out Brady for the romance, Smalls said it's mostly "about mourning a friendship that you thought was going to be everlasting.”
      
    
              As we reported ... Swanepoel said she had a ton of respect for Smalls despite the rumored tension between them -- though it sounds like that might not be reciprocated.

description:

                          Sued by Model Ellie Fallon ...
body:
Actress Casimere Jollette
                          Sued by Model Ellie Fallon ...
                          Allegedly Attacked Her in Park
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 25, 2026
                            6:00 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Actress Casimere Jollette allegedly attacked a model in a park and spread lies about her rumored relationship with David Harbour ... according to accusations made in a new lawsuit.
      
    
              Ellie Fallon -- a 28-year-old model from New York City -- reportedly filed the suit against Jollette ... claiming she was sitting on a park bench last December when she was confronted by the other star. The New York Post the first to report on the lawsuit's allegations.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              Fallon claims Jollette "intentionally, willfully, maliciously and without legal justification” threw hot water on her in Tribeca Park.
      

              She then claims Jollette "savagely" punched her repeatedly ... allegedly leaving her with injuries so bad she needed medical attention.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              To make matters worse, Fallon also alleges Jollette spread lies about her on Reddit ... claiming the latter woman claimed she and David Harbour engaged in an affair before he and Lily Allen split up.
      
    
              According to Fallon, Jollette wrote in her post, "Yes, she was in fact seeing David Harbour before their marriage and in fact DID split them up,” adding she allegedly learned the info from “prime sources."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              She allegedly added in the post, "She quite literally told my best friend that yes, she was in fact seeing David Harbour before their marriage and in fact DID split them up."
      
    
              Jollette's lawyer -- Bill McGovern -- has slammed the suit as having "no merit" ... adding that he looked forward to having it dismissed immediately. He also claimed Fallon previously brought her allegations to criminal court in a case that was ultimately dismissed and sealed.
      
    
              Jollette rose to fame on the hit Netflix show "Tiny Pretty Things" about the cutthroat environment at a ballet academy.
